subject: Mathematics
framework: National Curriculum in England (2014): Mathematics programmes of study, with EYFS Mathematics (Number; Numerical Patterns) for Reception
statusNote: Key stage statements were read and paraphrased from the gov.uk National Curriculum mathematics programmes of study (Key Stages 1 to 3) and the Reception goals from the EYFS statutory framework for group and school-based providers (version effective September 2026). Statutory content is set by key stage, not by year. The year allocation in the year map is a recommended sequence aligned to the school's existing unit names, not a statutory requirement. Year 1 was rebuilt in November 2026 to the TGA Year 1 Curriculum Pack: one unit per half term, following Tarbiyyah Primary's Cornerstones projects (2026-27 order), White Rose maths and Little Wandle phonics. Years 2 to 9 were rebuilt in November 2026 to the TGA curriculum packs (docs/curriculum-packs/y2.md to y9.md): one unit per half term, titled by half term so the portal planner places each one. November 2026 alignment with the school's own files: Years 7 to 9 keep the White Rose Secondary block order (block names only); each unit's resources name the matching lessons of the school's KS3 scheme, Pearson's generic KS3 Maths Progress (Second Edition), and week plans and founding-year notes follow docs/curriculum-packs/y7.md to y9.md. November 2026 alignment: Years 1 to 6 follow the Tarbiyyah Primary Long Term Plan 2026-27 project order, with content checked against the school's 2023-24 curriculum maps and maths long-term plan and Maths policy (White Rose); each Spring 1 to Summer 2 unit carries its week plan, resources and founding-year line.

purpose: Mathematics is a creative, connected discipline used in daily life, science, engineering, finance and work.
Pupils become fluent, with quick and accurate recall of core mathematics.
Pupils reason mathematically: conjecture, generalise, justify and prove.
Pupils solve routine and unfamiliar problems by breaking them into steps and persevering.

statements: Understand numbers to 10, including what each number is made of.
Recognise small quantities, up to 5, at a glance without counting.
Recall number bonds to 5 and some to 10, including doubles, without aids.
Count aloud beyond 20 and notice the pattern in the counting system.
Compare quantities to 10 using greater than, less than and equal to.
Explore patterns in numbers to 10: odd and even, doubles and equal sharing.
Count forwards and backwards, to and across 100, from any number.
Count in 2s, 5s and 10s; identify one more and one less.
Read and write numbers to 100 in numerals and words.
Compare and order numbers from 0 to 100 using <, > and =.
Read, write and interpret statements using +, - and =.
Know number bonds and related subtraction facts within 20.
Add and subtract one- and two-digit numbers, including with missing numbers.
Know addition can be done in any order but subtraction cannot.
Recall and use the 2, 5 and 10 multiplication tables.
Solve problems using arrays, repeated addition, sharing and grouping.
Recognise odd and even numbers; write statements using x, divide and =.
Recognise, find and name halves and quarters of shapes and quantities.
Recognise, find and write thirds and three-quarters of quantities.
Know that two-quarters is equal to one-half.
Compare, describe and measure length, mass, capacity and temperature using standard units.
Recognise coins and notes and solve simple money problems.
Tell the time to the hour, half hour and five minutes; sequence events.
Recognise and name common 2D and 3D shapes and describe their properties.
Describe position, direction and movement, including whole, half and quarter turns.
Order and arrange objects in patterns and sequences.
Interpret and construct pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams and tables.
Answer questions by counting and comparing categories.
Read, write, order and compare numbers to 1,000,000 and then 10,000,000.
Count in multiples of 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 25, 50, 100 and 1,000.
Use negative numbers in context and count through zero.
Round numbers to a required degree of accuracy; read Roman numerals.
Use formal written methods for all four operations with whole numbers.
Recall multiplication tables to 12 x 12 and use factor pairs.
Identify multiples, factors, primes, squares and cubes.
Use the order of operations and estimate to check answers.
Solve multi-step problems in context, choosing methods and interpreting remainders.
Recognise equivalent fractions and compare, order, add and subtract fractions.
Convert between mixed numbers and improper fractions; multiply and divide simple fractions.
Read, write, round and compare decimals to three places.
Understand percentages as parts per 100 and link fractions, decimals and percentages.
Solve problems about relative sizes of two quantities.
Calculate percentages and use them to compare.
Solve scale factor problems with similar shapes and unequal sharing.
Use simple formulae and generate linear number sequences.
Express missing number problems algebraically.
Find pairs of numbers satisfying an equation with two unknowns.
Convert between metric units and between miles and kilometres.
Find perimeter and area of rectilinear shapes, parallelograms and triangles.
Calculate and compare volumes of cubes and cuboids.
Read, write and convert time, including 12-hour and 24-hour clocks.
Classify triangles, quadrilaterals and polygons by their properties.
Know angle facts at a point, on a line and vertically opposite angles.
Draw shapes from dimensions and angles; build nets of 3D shapes.
Name circle parts and know diameter is twice the radius.
Describe positions using coordinates in the first quadrant, then all four quadrants.
Translate and reflect shapes on a coordinate grid.
Present and interpret data using bar charts, pictograms, tables and time graphs.
Interpret and construct line graphs and pie charts.
Calculate and interpret the mean as an average.
Develop fluency with number, algebra and representations, moving between them.
Reason: make and test conjectures; begin deductive reasoning, proof and counter-examples.
Solve multi-step problems, model situations and apply mathematics to finance.
Choose methods for unfamiliar problems and evaluate outcomes.
Understand place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size.
Use primes, factors, multiples, prime factorisation, HCF and LCM.
Apply the four operations to integers, decimals and fractions, including negatives.
Use order of operations, integer powers, roots and standard form.
Work with percentages including those above 100%, and with fractions as operators.
Round, estimate, and use calculators sensibly, including error intervals.
Use algebraic notation; substitute into formulae, including scientific formulae.
Simplify, expand and factorise; rearrange formulae to change the subject.
Solve linear equations and simultaneous linear equations graphically.
Use coordinates in four quadrants; sketch linear and quadratic graphs; use y = mx + c.
Generate sequences and find the nth term of arithmetic sequences.

strands.strand: Ratio, proportion and rates of change
statements: Convert between standard units and use scale factors, diagrams and maps.
Use ratio notation, simplify ratios and divide quantities in a given ratio.
Solve percentage change problems, including simple interest.
Solve direct and inverse proportion problems and use compound units.
Derive and use formulae for perimeter, area and volume, including circles and prisms.
Use ruler and compass constructions, congruence criteria and angle facts.
Use enlargement, Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometric ratios in right-angled triangles.
Describe translations, rotations and reflections and properties of 3D shapes.
Record and analyse outcome frequencies on the 0 to 1 probability scale.
Know that probabilities of all outcomes sum to 1.
Use tables, grids and Venn diagrams to list outcomes and calculate theoretical probabilities.
Describe, compare and interpret distributions using averages and measures of spread.
Construct and interpret frequency tables, bar charts, pie charts and pictograms.
Use scatter graphs to describe relationships between two variables.

toKS4: Key Stage 3 prepares pupils for Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A (4MA1), Higher tier, taught in Years 10 and 11 in the order of Pearson's two-year 4MA1 scheme of work. Number (place value, powers, roots, standard form, fractions, percentages) sets up 4MA1 Units 1 to 8 (spec section 1); algebra, sequences and graphs set up Units 9 to 19 (sections 2 and 3); angles, constructions, area, volume, Pythagoras, similarity and transformations set up Units 20 to 29 (sections 4 and 5); averages, charts and probability set up Units 30 to 32 (section 6). Year 9 ends with quadratic graphs, tree diagrams and an introduction to trigonometry so Year 10 can begin 4MA1 at pace.

gaps: The gov.uk programme-of-study page text was read up to 100,000 characters; the final few hundred characters (the closing notes) were not read.

Year-by-year allocation of units is a recommended sequence aligned to the school's existing unit names; the National Curriculum fixes content by key stage, except where the document names a year (Year 2 statistics, Year 6 ratio and algebra).

Reception year map units 'Numbers to 10 and number bonds' and 'Measures and time (early)' are additional recommended units; they follow the EYFS Number and Numerical Patterns goals but are not statutory unit titles.
Several Year 9 units that introduce GCSE content (quadratics, fractional indices, vectors) are recommended extensions beyond the strictly statutory KS3 list.
